paras: The attempted lynching of Brown and expulsion of Black residents from Whitesboro, Texas, took place in August 1903, when a white mob hanged a Black prisoner accused of attempting to assault a white woman and then drove much of the town's Black population out. Officers cut the man down alive, but the mob went on to whip men who stayed, and more than 100 Black residents were reported to have fled. In May 1904 the town's mayor was arrested on a federal indictment for conspiracy in the expulsion.

According to an Associated Press dispatch dated August 12, an attempted assault that day on Mrs. Hart, a white woman, led to the arrest of eight Black men, seven of whom were released while the eighth was held for identification. Later white reports added an alleged poisoning plot: the Jackson Herald said resolutions of an "antiwhite club" to poison wells had been found and blue-stone discovered in the depot water. A New Orleans dispatch in the New York Sun traced the trouble to a lynching in the town more than a year earlier, which Black residents had denounced, and to a paper purporting to propose poisoning the wells in revenge.

About 8 o'clock that evening a mob took the prisoner, by some accounts from the jail, and hanged him from the limb of a tree. By the wire account, officers from Sherman forced their way through the mob, cut him down before he lost consciousness and hurried him to Sherman. A separate Whitesboro dispatch named him as Brown and said the mob withdrew "believing they had accomplished their purpose."

The mob then turned on the town's Black residents, firing guns "promiscuously" in their section and ordering them to leave at once; outgoing trains were reported filled with Black passengers. By August 14, despite promises of protection, residents were still leaving, and several men had been severely flogged, houses entered and furniture destroyed. A Denison special to the St. Louis Republic reported that seventeen men who disregarded the order were publicly whipped on the night of August 15 and that armed white men patrolled the streets. The Sun put the mob at about 300, and by August 20 a Dallas dispatch said more than 100 Black residents had fled after notices were posted ordering them out.

United States marshals and county officers were sent to the town, and Grayson County authorities said they intended to arrest the mob's leaders and put the affair before the grand jury. The governor and local authorities were reported as pledging every effort to punish the mob. On May 20, 1904, Mayor J. W. M. Hughes was arrested at Sherman on a federal indictment charging conspiracy "to set at naught the civil rights bill" by forcibly expelling Black residents, and was released on $2,500 bond. No report of that case's outcome, of any indictment of mob members, or of Brown's later fate appears in the coverage.

The story spread through an Associated Press dispatch of August 13 from Savannah to Butte, under headlines such as "Mob Starts Reign of Terror" and "Mob Is Frantic." Later items turned to the expulsion and its supposed causes: the Portland Daily Press headed one dispatch "Whitesboro for Whites," and the St. Louis Republic ran "Seventeen Negroes Whipped by Citizens" with the subhead "Summary Action Follows." The Sun asked "Negro Poisoning Plot?" and presented the alleged plot as the riot's cause, while a San Antonio Daily Light digest called the prisoner "a man known to be innocent."

A Record-Herald dispatch from Dallas, reprinted in Utah and Nevada, ran as "Race War in Texas" and placed the events at "White Wright." Weekly news summaries carried the story into late August, and the mayor's arrest was reprinted in Alabama and Mississippi in 1904; no account was found in the Black press.

Reports disagreed on whether officers from Sherman or the sheriff and a posse made the rescue, and on whether Brown had lost consciousness. The number whipped was "several" in one dispatch and seventeen in the Republic's, and the Dallas dispatch named the town "Wright" or "Whitewright," though its details match Whitesboro. The poisoning-plot and earlier-lynching claims come only from white reports and are uncorroborated.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Brown and expulsion of Black residents from Whitesboro, Texas
bases: The mob hanged a prisoner who was cut down alive (A3, A6), then fired guns in the Black section, whipped men who stayed and posted notices ordering all Black residents out until more than 100 fled (A13, A16, A18), and the mayor was later federally indicted for the forced expulsion (A27); the attempted lynching was the trigger, the expulsion the main outcome.

A mob took an accused prisoner and hanged him for an alleged attempted assault on a white woman, but officers cut him down alive and he was taken to Sherman (A3, A6, A17); no one was reported killed, so this is an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

The AP wire (A3, A6), an independent Whitesboro dispatch (A17), a Denison special (A16), a New Orleans dispatch (A15) and a Dallas dispatch (A18) agree on the hanging, rescue and expulsion, and the 1904 federal indictment (A27) confirms the forced expulsion.

framing.detail: The AP dispatch ran nationally under headlines such as 'Mob Starts Reign of Terror', 'Mob Is Frantic' and 'Officers Cut Him Down After He Has Been Hanged by Lynchers'.
The St. Louis Republic headlined 'Seventeen Negroes Whipped by Citizens' with 'Summary Action Follows' and blamed assaults on white women and poisoned water.
The Sun ran 'Negro Poisoning Plot?' presenting an alleged plot as the cause, while reporting the plan to arrest mob leaders.
The San Antonio Daily Light's digest called the prisoner 'a man known to be innocent' saved by the officers.
The Record-Herald Dallas dispatch ran as 'Fleeing to Escape Death', 'Negroes Fear Race War' and 'Race War in Texas'.
